0. Overview

Basic Information

Instructor: Shelly Kagan

Recorded Autumn 2007

Open Yale Courses

Course Direction

The question this course asks is not the factual one, such as waht happens after death, but a chain of philosophical ones:

What is a person?

What is a death?

Why, if at all, is death bad? 

Is fear of death rational? 

Given that you must die, how should you live?

Under what conditions can suicide be rational, or even morally permissible?

Kagan works in the analytic style: 

• First cut the concepts clean: soul, body, person, death vs. dying vs. being dead.

• Then Lay out the best argument for each position in turn and look for the flaw.

His own leanings are physicalism plyus the deprivation account, but the course deliberatyely withholds a verdict. 

So the actually delivers is not a set of answers but the ability to tell a good argument from a bad one. 

Six Main Modules

What is a person: Dualism vs. Physicalism. The souls can be netiher observed nor introspected, so the only live defence is infrence to the best explanation: find a a feature that physicalism cannot explain and that positing a soul explains better. 

Plato’s arguments for immortality: Some arguments: from the soul’s bringing lifew and admitting no death, tp the claim that only composites can be destroyed adn the soul is simple. 

Personal identity: What keeps you the same person overtime? The module ends in a turn: perhaps identity itself is not what matters. 

The nature of death and believing you will die: Death is not a state but a terminus. Imaginging my death as something I undergo is a trick of the imagination. 

The badness of death: If death is the end, what is bad about it? The deprivation account: death is bas because it deprives you of goods you would otherwise have had - so dying young if worse than dying old, and immortality may not be good at all (reptition, boredom, the dilution of a life’s value). 

Fear, living, suicide: Does fear of death have an object - the satte of being dead, or the process of dying? If death is annihilation, is fear of it simply irrational?
